## 1. Scope & Inputs This cycle covers cycle i14-2026-10-s2 for Project SDLC and two selected Requirements: SDLC-FR-0201 (every stored event record, including its payload, must be permanently deleted seven days after it was received) and SDLC-FR-0202 (every stored event record, including its payload, must remain retrievable unchanged for at least ninety days after it was received). The UX decision is recorded as NOT_APPLICABLE: this is a back-end service with no user-facing surface. Both Requirements exclude backups. Both apply to every event record in the event store without exception, so they directly contradict each other. Any record aged between seven and ninety days would have to be both deleted and retrievable. No architecture can satisfy both as written. This document therefore defines one integrated design for the event store's record lifecycle: ingestion with a trusted receipt time, retrieval, and age-based permanent deletion. That design does not depend on which product decision resolves the conflict. The contradiction is recorded as a material product question and is not resolved here. The architecture does not choose either retention period, and it does not treat either Requirement as taking precedence. ## 2. Resolution depends on a material product question. | ## 3. Solution Structure The solution is a single back-end event-store service with three logical parts. The ingestion path accepts event records and stamps each one with an authoritative received-at timestamp. The retrieval path serves records by identifier or by query, and it refuses to return any record whose age is past the governing deletion horizon. The retention enforcement path is a scheduled lifecycle process that permanently removes records, payloads included, once they pass that horizon. All three paths share one lifecycle policy definition. That definition holds the minimum availability window and the deletion horizon, both measured from received-at. Because there is only one source for the policy, retrieval-time filtering and physical deletion cannot disagree. Once the product question is answered, the governing values are set in this definition. Until then, the design does not encode either seven days or ninety days as authoritative. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Ingestion Service: validates incoming event records, assigns the authoritative received-at timestamp from the service clock (never from producer-supplied time), and persists the record and its payload atomically. Event Store: the persistent store for record metadata and payloads. It is organized by received-at so that age-based deletion is efficient and complete. Retrieval Service: returns records unchanged, as they were persisted. It excludes any record whose received-at is older than the deletion horizon, so expired records are unretrievable even before the physical purge has run. Lifecycle Policy: one versioned definition of the availability window and the deletion horizon. It is read by the Retrieval Service and the Retention Enforcer, and its consistency is validated at startup: the horizon must not be shorter than the availability window. Retention Enforcer: a scheduled job that permanently deletes every record and payload past the horizon, including copies held in secondary indexes or caches within the event store, and records what it deleted. Clock Source: a synchronized time source used by both ingestion and enforcement so that ages are computed consistently. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Ingest flow: a producer submits an event to the Ingestion Service. The service stamps received-at, writes the metadata and payload to the Event Store in one atomic operation, and acknowledges the producer with the record identifier. Retrieve flow: a consumer requests a record by identifier, or queries by time range. The Retrieval Service reads from the Event Store, applies the Lifecycle Policy horizon filter, and returns the record unchanged, or not-found if the record is absent or expired. Not-found is indistinguishable for absent and expired records, so expired data is not leaked through existence probing. Enforcement flow: on each scheduled run, the Retention Enforcer reads the horizon from the Lifecycle Policy, computes a cutoff from the Clock Source, permanently deletes all records and payloads whose received-at is before the cutoff, and emits the counts and the oldest remaining received-at to observability. Policy flow: the Lifecycle Policy is loaded at service start and validated. A change to it is a governed release event, not a runtime toggle. ## 6. Data / Storage Each event record holds an immutable identifier, an immutable received-at timestamp, metadata, and a payload. The payload is stored with the record, or in a payload store that shares the record's lifecycle, so that deletion is atomic. Payloads are never modified after write, which preserves the unchanged-retrieval property. Storage is partitioned by received-at, for example in time-bucketed partitions. This lets the Retention Enforcer delete whole expired partitions, which makes deletion complete and cheap and avoids leftover rows. Deletion is permanent within the event store, including derived indexes and any internal caches. Backups are out of scope under both Requirements' Non-Goals. Capacity must be sized for the longer of the candidate windows until the product question is resolved, because the volume retained differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between seven and ninety days. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — The Requirements define no external systems; producers and consumers interact only through the service's ingest and retrieve interfaces. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Producers and consumers authenticate to the ingest and retrieve interfaces using the platform's standard service-to-service authentication. Authorization separates the right to ingest from the right to retrieve. Only the Retention Enforcer's identity may perform deletion, and no external interface exposes deletion or changes to retention. Changes to the Lifecycle Policy go through the governed release process, because altering it changes both the availability and the deletion guarantees. Expired records are reported as not-found exactly like absent records, so record existence is not disclosed after the deletion horizon. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model The Ingestion and Retrieval Services run as stateless, horizontally scalable instances in front of the Event Store. The Retention Enforcer runs as a single-active scheduled job, guarded by a lease, so that concurrent runs cannot conflict. It runs often enough that physical deletion lags the horizon by no more than one scheduling interval. Retrieval-time filtering already makes expired records unretrievable, so that lag never makes an expired record retrievable. All components use the same synchronized Clock Source. ## 10. Failure / Recovery If an enforcement run fails or is skipped, records past the horizon remain physically present but stay unretrievable because of retrieval-time filtering. The next run is idempotent and deletes everything past the cutoff, so missed runs are caught up automatically. Partition-level deletion is atomic per partition, so a partial run leaves no half-deleted records. An ingest write is acknowledged only after the record and its payload are durably persisted, so no acknowledged record is lost inside the availability window. If the Lifecycle Policy fails startup validation, the service refuses to start instead of running with an inconsistent policy. Clock skew is bounded by the synchronized Clock Source, and enforcement applies its cutoff using the service's own received-at values only. ## 11. Observability The service emits the following metrics: the age of the oldest physically present record and of the oldest retrievable record, records and bytes deleted per enforcement run, the time of the last successful enforcement run, enforcement failures, and the number of retrieval requests answered not-found because the record had expired. Alerts fire in three cases: the oldest physically present record exceeds the horizon by more than one scheduling interval, an enforcement run fails, or the oldest retrievable record is younger than the availability window while the store has been running longer than that window, which indicates premature loss. These signals provide the operational evidence for whichever acceptance criteria end up governing. ## 12. Migration Implications N/A — The selected Requirements and inputs describe no existing event store or data, so no migration is in scope. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1: there is one integrated lifecycle design and no choice between the conflicting Requirements. SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 cannot both hold for records aged between seven and ninety days. Choosing a period would answer a product question, which is outside the Architect's authority, so the conflict is raised as a material product question. The trade-off is that the architecture cannot be declared to satisfy both Requirements until the conflict is resolved. Decision 2: a single Lifecycle Policy is shared by retrieval and enforcement, and it is validated at startup. This prevents the deletion horizon and the availability window from drifting apart. The cost is that retention changes must go through a governed release. Decision 3: retrieval-time filtering is combined with scheduled physical deletion. Expired records become unretrievable exactly at the horizon without requiring real-time deletion. The cost is a bounded window in which expired data still exists physically, although it cannot be retrieved. Decision 4: storage is partitioned by received-at, with partition-level purge. Deletion becomes complete, atomic and cheap. The cost is coarser deletion granularity, so the partition size must be no larger than the enforcement interval. Decision 5: received-at is assigned by the service, not taken from the producer. This gives every record a consistent and tamper-resistant age. The cost is that producer event time is not used for retention. ## 14. Assumptions - Received-at means the time the event store service accepted and durably persisted the record, not any producer-supplied event time. - The event store is a single logical store owned by this service, and no other system holds primary copies of event records. - Producers and consumers can authenticate using the platform's standard service-to-service mechanism. ## 15. Risks - SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 directly contradict each other for records aged between seven and ninety days. Until the contradiction is resolved, no implementation can pass both acceptance criteria. — Impact: HIGH - Storage capacity differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between the two candidate windows. Sizing for the wrong one risks either overspending or running out of capacity. — Impact: MEDIUM - Copies of records outside the event store, such as caches in consumers or downstream exports, are not covered by in-store deletion. They could undermine the deletion intent even though backups are explicitly excluded. — Impact: MEDIUM ## 16. # SDLC-FR-0201 — Delete event records after seven days

## Requirement

Every stored event record must be permanently deleted seven days after it was received.

## Detailed Behavior

Deletion applies to all event records in the event store, including their payloads; a deleted record cannot be retrieved.

## Rationale

Stored events must not be kept longer than necessary.

## Acceptance / Verification

An event record received more than seven days ago cannot be retrieved.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Applies to every event record without exception.

## Non-Goals

Does not cover backups.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0202 — Retain event records for ninety days

## Requirement

Every stored event record must remain available for retrieval for at least ninety days after it was received.

## Detailed Behavior

Retention applies to all event records in the event store, including their payloads; retrieval within ninety days returns the record unchanged.

## Rationale

Consumers need to re-read events during investigations.

## Acceptance / Verification

An event record received eighty days ago can still be retrieved unchanged.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Applies to every event record without exception.

## Non-Goals

Does not cover backups.

## Open Questions

None.

Resolution depends on a material product question. | ## 3. Solution Structure The solution is a single back-end event-store service with three logical parts. The ingestion path accepts event records and stamps each one with an authoritative received-at timestamp. The retrieval path serves records by identifier or by query, and it refuses to return any record whose age is past the governing deletion horizon. The retention enforcement path is a scheduled lifecycle process that permanently removes records, payloads included, once they pass that horizon. All three paths share one lifecycle policy definition. That definition holds the minimum availability window and the deletion horizon, both measured from received-at. Because there is only one source for the policy, retrieval-time filtering and physical deletion cannot disagree. Once the product question is answered, the governing values are set in this definition. Until then, the design does not encode either seven days or ninety days as authoritative. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Ingestion Service: validates incoming event records, assigns the authoritative received-at timestamp from the service clock (never from producer-supplied time), and persists the record and its payload atomically. Event Store: the persistent store for record metadata and payloads. It is organized by received-at so that age-based deletion is efficient and complete. Retrieval Service: returns records unchanged, as they were persisted. It excludes any record whose received-at is older than the deletion horizon, so expired records are unretrievable even before the physical purge has run. Lifecycle Policy: one versioned definition of the availability window and the deletion horizon. It is read by the Retrieval Service and the Retention Enforcer, and its consistency is validated at startup: the horizon must not be shorter than the availability window. Retention Enforcer: a scheduled job that permanently deletes every record and payload past the horizon, including copies held in secondary indexes or caches within the event store, and records what it deleted. Clock Source: a synchronized time source used by both ingestion and enforcement so that ages are computed consistently. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Ingest flow: a producer submits an event to the Ingestion Service. The service stamps received-at, writes the metadata and payload to the Event Store in one atomic operation, and acknowledges the producer with the record identifier. Retrieve flow: a consumer requests a record by identifier, or queries by time range. The Retrieval Service reads from the Event Store, applies the Lifecycle Policy horizon filter, and returns the record unchanged, or not-found if the record is absent or expired. Not-found is indistinguishable for absent and expired records, so expired data is not leaked through existence probing. Enforcement flow: on each scheduled run, the Retention Enforcer reads the horizon from the Lifecycle Policy, computes a cutoff from the Clock Source, permanently deletes all records and payloads whose received-at is before the cutoff, and emits the counts and the oldest remaining received-at to observability. Policy flow: the Lifecycle Policy is loaded at service start and validated. A change to it is a governed release event, not a runtime toggle. ## 6. Data / Storage Each event record holds an immutable identifier, an immutable received-at timestamp, metadata, and a payload. The payload is stored with the record, or in a payload store that shares the record's lifecycle, so that deletion is atomic. Payloads are never modified after write, which preserves the unchanged-retrieval property. Storage is partitioned by received-at, for example in time-bucketed partitions. This lets the Retention Enforcer delete whole expired partitions, which makes deletion complete and cheap and avoids leftover rows. Deletion is permanent within the event store, including derived indexes and any internal caches. Backups are out of scope under both Requirements' Non-Goals. Capacity must be sized for the longer of the candidate windows until the product question is resolved, because the volume retained differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between seven and ninety days. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — The Requirements define no external systems; producers and consumers interact only through the service's ingest and retrieve interfaces. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Producers and consumers authenticate to the ingest and retrieve interfaces using the platform's standard service-to-service authentication. Authorization separates the right to ingest from the right to retrieve. Only the Retention Enforcer's identity may perform deletion, and no external interface exposes deletion or changes to retention. Changes to the Lifecycle Policy go through the governed release process, because altering it changes both the availability and the deletion guarantees. Expired records are reported as not-found exactly like absent records, so record existence is not disclosed after the deletion horizon. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model The Ingestion and Retrieval Services run as stateless, horizontally scalable instances in front of the Event Store. The Retention Enforcer runs as a single-active scheduled job, guarded by a lease, so that concurrent runs cannot conflict. It runs often enough that physical deletion lags the horizon by no more than one scheduling interval. Retrieval-time filtering already makes expired records unretrievable, so that lag never makes an expired record retrievable. All components use the same synchronized Clock Source. ## 10. Failure / Recovery If an enforcement run fails or is skipped, records past the horizon remain physically present but stay unretrievable because of retrieval-time filtering. The next run is idempotent and deletes everything past the cutoff, so missed runs are caught up automatically. Partition-level deletion is atomic per partition, so a partial run leaves no half-deleted records. An ingest write is acknowledged only after the record and its payload are durably persisted, so no acknowledged record is lost inside the availability window. If the Lifecycle Policy fails startup validation, the service refuses to start instead of running with an inconsistent policy. Clock skew is bounded by the synchronized Clock Source, and enforcement applies its cutoff using the service's own received-at values only. ## 11. Observability The service emits the following metrics: the age of the oldest physically present record and of the oldest retrievable record, records and bytes deleted per enforcement run, the time of the last successful enforcement run, enforcement failures, and the number of retrieval requests answered not-found because the record had expired. Alerts fire in three cases: the oldest physically present record exceeds the horizon by more than one scheduling interval, an enforcement run fails, or the oldest retrievable record is younger than the availability window while the store has been running longer than that window, which indicates premature loss. These signals provide the operational evidence for whichever acceptance criteria end up governing. ## 12. Migration Implications N/A — The selected Requirements and inputs describe no existing event store or data, so no migration is in scope. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1: there is one integrated lifecycle design and no choice between the conflicting Requirements. SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 cannot both hold for records aged between seven and ninety days. Choosing a period would answer a product question, which is outside the Architect's authority, so the conflict is raised as a material product question. The trade-off is that the architecture cannot be declared to satisfy both Requirements until the conflict is resolved. Decision 2: a single Lifecycle Policy is shared by retrieval and enforcement, and it is validated at startup. This prevents the deletion horizon and the availability window from drifting apart. The cost is that retention changes must go through a governed release. Decision 3: retrieval-time filtering is combined with scheduled physical deletion. Expired records become unretrievable exactly at the horizon without requiring real-time deletion. The cost is a bounded window in which expired data still exists physically, although it cannot be retrieved. Decision 4: storage is partitioned by received-at, with partition-level purge. Deletion becomes complete, atomic and cheap. The cost is coarser deletion granularity, so the partition size must be no larger than the enforcement interval. Decision 5: received-at is assigned by the service, not taken from the producer. This gives every record a consistent and tamper-resistant age. The cost is that producer event time is not used for retention. ## 14. Assumptions - Received-at means the time the event store service accepted and durably persisted the record, not any producer-supplied event time. - The event store is a single logical store owned by this service, and no other system holds primary copies of event records. - Producers and consumers can authenticate using the platform's standard service-to-service mechanism. ## 15. Risks - SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 directly contradict each other for records aged between seven and ninety days. Until the contradiction is resolved, no implementation can pass both acceptance criteria. — Impact: HIGH - Storage capacity differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between the two candidate windows. assumptions: Received-at means the time the event store service accepted and durably persisted the record, not any producer-supplied event time.
The event store is a single logical store owned by this service, and no other system holds primary copies of event records.
Producers and consumers can authenticate using the platform's standard service-to-service mechanism.
open_architecture_questions: What enforcement scheduling interval and partition granularity are acceptable for the gap between logical expiry and physical deletion, once the governing horizon is known?

product_questions.detail: SDLC-FR-0201 requires every event record to be permanently deleted seven days after receipt, while SDLC-FR-0202 requires every event record to remain retrievable for at least ninety days after receipt. Both apply without exception. Which obligation governs, or do the two Requirements apply to different classes of event records that the Requirements do not yet distinguish?

SDLC-FR-0202 conflicts with SDLC-FR-0201: ninety-day minimum availability versus deletion at seven days, both applied to every event record without exception. Which obligation governs, or how is the scope of each Requirement to be separated?

risks.detail: SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 directly contradict each other for records aged between seven and ninety days. Until the contradiction is resolved, no implementation can pass both acceptance criteria.
Storage capacity differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between the two candidate windows. Sizing for the wrong one risks either overspending or running out of capacity.

Copies of records outside the event store, such as caches in consumers or downstream exports, are not covered by in-store deletion. They could undermine the deletion intent even though backups are explicitly excluded.

sections.architecture_decisions: Decision 1: there is one integrated lifecycle design and no choice between the conflicting Requirements. SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 cannot both hold for records aged between seven and ninety days. Choosing a period would answer a product question, which is outside the Architect's authority, so the conflict is raised as a material product question. The trade-off is that the architecture cannot be declared to satisfy both Requirements until the conflict is resolved. Decision 2: a single Lifecycle Policy is shared by retrieval and enforcement, and it is validated at startup. This prevents the deletion horizon and the availability window from drifting apart. The cost is that retention changes must go through a governed release. Decision 3: retrieval-time filtering is combined with scheduled physical deletion. Expired records become unretrievable exactly at the horizon without requiring real-time deletion. The cost is a bounded window in which expired data still exists physically, although it cannot be retrieved. Decision 4: storage is partitioned by received-at, with partition-level purge. Deletion becomes complete, atomic and cheap. The cost is coarser deletion granularity, so the partition size must be no larger than the enforcement interval. Decision 5: received-at is assigned by the service, not taken from the producer. This gives every record a consistent and tamper-resistant age. The cost is that producer event time is not used for retention.
sections.components_and_responsibilities: Ingestion Service: validates incoming event records, assigns the authoritative received-at timestamp from the service clock (never from producer-supplied time), and persists the record and its payload atomically. Event Store: the persistent store for record metadata and payloads. It is organized by received-at so that age-based deletion is efficient and complete. Retrieval Service: returns records unchanged, as they were persisted. It excludes any record whose received-at is older than the deletion horizon, so expired records are unretrievable even before the physical purge has run. Lifecycle Policy: one versioned definition of the availability window and the deletion horizon. It is read by the Retrieval Service and the Retention Enforcer, and its consistency is validated at startup: the horizon must not be shorter than the availability window. Retention Enforcer: a scheduled job that permanently deletes every record and payload past the horizon, including copies held in secondary indexes or caches within the event store, and records what it deleted. Clock Source: a synchronized time source used by both ingestion and enforcement so that ages are computed consistently.
sections.data_storage: Each event record holds an immutable identifier, an immutable received-at timestamp, metadata, and a payload. The payload is stored with the record, or in a payload store that shares the record's lifecycle, so that deletion is atomic. Payloads are never modified after write, which preserves the unchanged-retrieval property. Storage is partitioned by received-at, for example in time-bucketed partitions. This lets the Retention Enforcer delete whole expired partitions, which makes deletion complete and cheap and avoids leftover rows. Deletion is permanent within the event store, including derived indexes and any internal caches. Backups are out of scope under both Requirements' Non-Goals. Capacity must be sized for the longer of the candidate windows until the product question is resolved, because the volume retained differs by roughly a factor of thirteen between seven and ninety days.
sections.deployment_runtime_model: The Ingestion and Retrieval Services run as stateless, horizontally scalable instances in front of the Event Store. The Retention Enforcer runs as a single-active scheduled job, guarded by a lease, so that concurrent runs cannot conflict. It runs often enough that physical deletion lags the horizon by no more than one scheduling interval. Retrieval-time filtering already makes expired records unretrievable, so that lag never makes an expired record retrievable. All components use the same synchronized Clock Source.
sections.external_integrations: N/A — The Requirements define no external systems; producers and consumers interact only through the service's ingest and retrieve interfaces.
sections.failure_recovery: If an enforcement run fails or is skipped, records past the horizon remain physically present but stay unretrievable because of retrieval-time filtering. The next run is idempotent and deletes everything past the cutoff, so missed runs are caught up automatically. Partition-level deletion is atomic per partition, so a partial run leaves no half-deleted records. An ingest write is acknowledged only after the record and its payload are durably persisted, so no acknowledged record is lost inside the availability window. If the Lifecycle Policy fails startup validation, the service refuses to start instead of running with an inconsistent policy. Clock skew is bounded by the synchronized Clock Source, and enforcement applies its cutoff using the service's own received-at values only.
sections.interfaces_and_data_flows: Ingest flow: a producer submits an event to the Ingestion Service. The service stamps received-at, writes the metadata and payload to the Event Store in one atomic operation, and acknowledges the producer with the record identifier. Retrieve flow: a consumer requests a record by identifier, or queries by time range. The Retrieval Service reads from the Event Store, applies the Lifecycle Policy horizon filter, and returns the record unchanged, or not-found if the record is absent or expired. Not-found is indistinguishable for absent and expired records, so expired data is not leaked through existence probing. Enforcement flow: on each scheduled run, the Retention Enforcer reads the horizon from the Lifecycle Policy, computes a cutoff from the Clock Source, permanently deletes all records and payloads whose received-at is before the cutoff, and emits the counts and the oldest remaining received-at to observability. Policy flow: the Lifecycle Policy is loaded at service start and validated. A change to it is a governed release event, not a runtime toggle.
sections.migration_implications: N/A — The selected Requirements and inputs describe no existing event store or data, so no migration is in scope.
sections.observability: The service emits the following metrics: the age of the oldest physically present record and of the oldest retrievable record, records and bytes deleted per enforcement run, the time of the last successful enforcement run, enforcement failures, and the number of retrieval requests answered not-found because the record had expired. Alerts fire in three cases: the oldest physically present record exceeds the horizon by more than one scheduling interval, an enforcement run fails, or the oldest retrievable record is younger than the availability window while the store has been running longer than that window, which indicates premature loss. These signals provide the operational evidence for whichever acceptance criteria end up governing.
sections.scope_and_inputs: This cycle covers cycle i14-2026-10-s2 for Project SDLC and two selected Requirements: SDLC-FR-0201 (every stored event record, including its payload, must be permanently deleted seven days after it was received) and SDLC-FR-0202 (every stored event record, including its payload, must remain retrievable unchanged for at least ninety days after it was received). The UX decision is recorded as NOT_APPLICABLE: this is a back-end service with no user-facing surface. Both Requirements exclude backups. Both apply to every event record in the event store without exception, so they directly contradict each other. Any record aged between seven and ninety days would have to be both deleted and retrievable. No architecture can satisfy both as written. This document therefore defines one integrated design for the event store's record lifecycle: ingestion with a trusted receipt time, retrieval, and age-based permanent deletion. That design does not depend on which product decision resolves the conflict. The contradiction is recorded as a material product question and is not resolved here. The architecture does not choose either retention period, and it does not treat either Requirement as taking precedence.
sections.security_authn_authz: Producers and consumers authenticate to the ingest and retrieve interfaces using the platform's standard service-to-service authentication. Authorization separates the right to ingest from the right to retrieve. Only the Retention Enforcer's identity may perform deletion, and no external interface exposes deletion or changes to retention. Changes to the Lifecycle Policy go through the governed release process, because altering it changes both the availability and the deletion guarantees. Expired records are reported as not-found exactly like absent records, so record existence is not disclosed after the deletion horizon.
sections.solution_structure: The solution is a single back-end event-store service with three logical parts. The ingestion path accepts event records and stamps each one with an authoritative received-at timestamp. The retrieval path serves records by identifier or by query, and it refuses to return any record whose age is past the governing deletion horizon. The retention enforcement path is a scheduled lifecycle process that permanently removes records, payloads included, once they pass that horizon. All three paths share one lifecycle policy definition. That definition holds the minimum availability window and the deletion horizon, both measured from received-at. Because there is only one source for the policy, retrieval-time filtering and physical deletion cannot disagree. Once the product question is answered, the governing values are set in this definition. Until then, the design does not encode either seven days or ninety days as authoritative.

constraints: Applies to every event record and payload in the event store without exception.
gaps: Cannot be satisfied together with SDLC-FR-0202: a seven-day deletion horizon prevents ninety-day availability. Resolution depends on a material product question.
traceability.how_satisfied: The Retention Enforcer permanently deletes records and payloads, using partition-level purge, once they pass the Lifecycle Policy deletion horizon measured from the service-assigned received-at. The Retrieval Service filters out records past that horizon so they cannot be retrieved. With a horizon of seven days, this satisfies the Requirement in isolation.

constraints: Applies to every event record and payload in the event store without exception.
gaps: Cannot be satisfied together with SDLC-FR-0201: ninety-day availability prevents deletion at seven days. Resolution depends on a material product question.

The Lifecycle Policy availability window, validated so that it is never longer than the deletion horizon, keeps records retrievable for at least the window. With a window of ninety days, this satisfies the Requirement in isolation.

# SDLC-FR-0201 — Delete event records after seven days

## Requirement

Every stored event record must be permanently deleted seven days after it was received.

## Detailed Behavior

Deletion applies to all event records in the event store, including their payloads; a deleted record cannot be retrieved.

## Rationale

Stored events must not be kept longer than necessary.

## Acceptance / Verification

An event record received more than seven days ago cannot be retrieved.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Applies to every event record without exception.

## Non-Goals

Does not cover backups.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0202 — Retain event records for ninety days

## Requirement

Every stored event record must remain available for retrieval for at least ninety days after it was received.

## Detailed Behavior

Retention applies to all event records in the event store, including their payloads; retrieval within ninety days returns the record unchanged.

## Rationale

Consumers need to re-read events during investigations.

## Acceptance / Verification

An event record received eighty days ago can still be retrieved unchanged.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Applies to every event record without exception.

## Non-Goals

Does not cover backups.

## Open Questions

None.

Retrieval filtering and enforcement read the same policy. The deletion-lag bound is inconsistent: tsa-s09 states at most one scheduling interval, and tsa-s11 alerts on that bound, but whole-partition purge (tsa-s06, tsa-s13 Decision 4) allows a lag of up to partition width plus interval. tsa-s01's claim of independence from the product resolution is not borne out for a class-separation resolution.

The satisfaction claims are limited to 'in isolation', and the mutual conflict is recorded as a gap in each row. The constraints match the sources. claim_verifications.reason: SDLC-FR-0201 requires every stored event record, including its payload, to be permanently deleted seven days after receipt, and its acceptance criterion says a record received more than seven days ago cannot be retrieved. SDLC-FR-0202 requires every stored event record to remain retrievable unchanged for at least ninety days, and its acceptance criterion says a record received eighty days ago can still be retrieved. Both apply to every event record in the event store without exception. Neither excludes the other's records; both exclude only backups. A record aged between seven and ninety days, such as the eighty-day record in SDLC-FR-0202's acceptance criterion, must be both unretrievable and retrievable. No implementation can pass both acceptance criteria.

Retained volume scales with the retention period, and ninety days divided by seven days is about 12.9. The factor of roughly thirteen is arithmetically correct at a constant ingest rate. The governing period is undetermined while the contradiction between SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 stands, so the sizing uncertainty is real. It is a consequence of the contradiction, not an independent defect.

SDLC-FR-0201 scopes deletion to 'all event records in the event store', so copies outside the event store fall outside its normative scope. The supplied sources say nothing about whether consumers cache retrieved records or whether downstream exports exist. They also give no way to tell whether such copies would conflict with the Requirement's rationale. The sources cannot settle whether this risk exists.

This is a genuine HOW question. SDLC-FR-0201 requires permanent deletion at seven days, while its acceptance criterion tests only that the record cannot be retrieved. The architecture uses logical expiry through retrieval filtering and later physical purge, so the scheduling interval and partition granularity determine how long expired data physically persists. The Requirements do not fix this tolerance. The question depends on the governing horizon, which in turn depends on the open product question.

Neither SDLC-FR-0201 nor SDLC-FR-0202 says which obligation governs. Neither distinguishes classes of event records: both say they apply to every event record without exception, and both record 'Open Questions: None'. No selected Requirement answers the question, so it remains a material product question.

This is the same conflict, raised against SDLC-FR-0202. The ninety-day minimum availability cannot coexist with deletion at seven days for the same records. Neither Requirement separates scope or establishes precedence, so the question is material and unanswered by the sources.

material_unresolved_what.detail: For records aged between seven and ninety days after receipt, it is not decided whether the seven-day permanent deletion obligation or the ninety-day minimum availability obligation governs, or whether the obligations apply to distinct classes of event records that the Requirements do not yet distinguish. The governing deletion horizon, the availability window, capacity sizing and lifecycle-policy structure all depend on this decision.

It is not decided whether the ninety-day minimum retrievability of every event record governs over SDLC-FR-0201's seven-day permanent deletion, or how the scope of each Requirement is separated. The correct availability window and the design of the lifecycle policy depend on this decision.

new_findings.detail: SDLC-FR-0201 (permanent deletion of every event record and payload seven days after receipt) and SDLC-FR-0202 (every event record and payload retrievable unchanged for at least ninety days after receipt) contradict each other for every record aged between seven and ninety days. Both apply without exception, and both exclude only backups.

tsa-s09 states that physical deletion lags the horizon by no more than one scheduling interval. tsa-s11 alerts when the oldest physically present record exceeds the horizon by more than one scheduling interval. However, tsa-s06 and tsa-s13 Decision 4 use whole-partition purge, with partition size bounded only by being no larger than the enforcement interval. Under whole-partition purge, a partition can be removed only once its newest record has passed the horizon; removing it earlier would delete unexpired records. The oldest record in a partition can therefore remain physically present for up to one partition width plus one scheduling interval past the horizon. That bound is up to twice the lag tsa-s09 states, and it would trigger the tsa-s11 alert during normal operation. This affects how closely physical deletion tracks SDLC-FR-0201's 'permanently deleted seven days after it was received'.

tsa-s01 asserts that the integrated design does not depend on which product decision resolves the conflict. The architecture's own product questions allow a resolution in which SDLC-FR-0201 and SDLC-FR-0202 apply to different classes of event records. The design provides a single Lifecycle Policy with one availability window and one deletion horizon (tsa-s03, tsa-s04). Its startup validation requires the horizon to be no shorter than the window. Ingestion assigns no record class. Under a class-separation resolution, the design as described cannot apply different lifecycles to different records, so its independence from the resolution holds only for resolutions that pick a single pair of global values.

SDLC-FR-0201's requirement text says 'permanently deleted seven days after it was received'. The architecture meets this at the horizon only logically, through retrieval filtering, and performs physical permanent deletion after a bounded lag (tsa-s09, tsa-s10, tsa-s13 Decision 3). This satisfies the stated acceptance criterion, which tests retrievability. The architecture acknowledges the gap with the requirement text's 'permanently deleted' through its open architecture question; the Requirement does not define a tolerance for that gap.

The architecture does not define boundary semantics at exactly the horizon: whether a record whose age equals the horizon is retrievable, and at what time granularity age is computed. The Requirements say 'more than seven days ago' (SDLC-FR-0201 acceptance) and 'at least ninety days' (SDLC-FR-0202). Precise boundary handling determines conformance at the edges once a governing period is set.
